title: Styles and design
summary:
This part settles how RichView looks: the brand layer, the five report styles and the default, how far authors may change a style, colour, typography, layout, surfaces and marks, chart chrome, motion outside chart behaviour, the site's look, and one set of design rules to replace the four texts that drift today. Chart behaviour lives in part 04a, report blocks in 04b and style-file types in 05; cards here decide values and looks and point to those items where they meet.

Daniel has answered the five key cards: STY-01 (the brand is only the RichView wordmark and the brand blue, in a distinct shade per style; the five styles differ in structure as well as faces and colours, each with its own design review; the site and RichView's presentations use one simple style; the June identity is retired), STY-05 (five styles, Sleek, Air, Scientific, Brutalist and Hand-drawn, with the studio variants kept as extended themes outside the normal menus), STY-06 (Sleek is the default everywhere; print and PDF use Air), STY-14 (rich style files: whatever differs between the styles can be changed, mechanics such as page width cannot, and agents are told which settings are safe and which experimental) and STY-68 (one review sheet per style, showing a representative majority of chart types, the map, flow, a normal and a pivot table and the flagship, with the other four styles beside it, judged first by a review agent). Daniel's INT-12 answer sets the craft and motion bar for every style: delightful and smooth, with the whimsy of Studio Ghibli and the polish of Apple's website animations.

The open decisions that matter most: STY-02 (the brand blue and each style's accent), STY-09 (Sleek cool as shipped or Lamplight warm), STY-10 (what sets Air apart from Sleek), STY-15 and STY-53 (the named settings over the rich style file, and authors' own colours checked at render), STY-20 and STY-22 (one colour scheme per style; the palette rule checks every pair of the first four colours), and STY-33 (whether Brutalist gets back the filled knockout panel Daniel liked in June).

How to answer: **accept** keeps a proposal as written, **edit** rewrites it, **reject** drops it from the rewrite, **defer** leaves it open. The five style cards (STY-09 to STY-13) list what ships at `b4db233` and end with every change other cards propose for that style; editing a value there changes that style. Screenshots come from `b4db233` builds and the live site on 2026-10-21 and 2026-10-22; colour figures were recomputed from the token values on 2026-10-22. Sources named "Daniel's notes" are pre-Notion notes kept on Claw Mini (see `evidence/intent-notion-site.md`). Part 08's cross-part contradiction cards (OPN-50 to OPN-68) decide conflicts involving this part's cards and should be answered first.

items.title: One brand, five report voices
items.question: Is RichView's look one house identity, or a brand layer over a family of distinct report styles?
items.why: Every other card in this part depends on it. June produced one house identity in two versions: the 2026-06-09 note, "The Economist meets Linear" (warm sand at hue 40, one indigo accent, Inter with Geist Mono), and the 2026-06-20 study, which kept warm paper and indigo 277, chose Newsreader with IBM Plex Mono and rejected the phrase as a vibe. Daniel's 2026-06-21 brief then asked for templates that each have a "different font, main accent", and S27-616 for five distinct identities. The house identity still lives in the base stylesheet's fallbacks, the legal pages' tokens, the showcase snapshot and the July `CLAUDE.md` in the primary checkout.
items.proposed: RichView has one brand layer — the name, the mark, the brand blue `#1A6DAC` and the site's paper-and-ink look — over five report styles, each a complete voice with its own faces, colours, type scale and marks. Inside a report the name and mark appear only in the colophon (STY-04); Scientific's accent is the brand blue (STY-02), as that style's colour rather than a brand badge. The June house identity is retired: its warm-sand and indigo fallbacks, legal-page tokens and showcase snapshot are deleted (STY-05, STY-17, STY-46).

items.title: The mark and the wordmark
items.question: How is the mark drawn, which wordmark goes with it, and which colours may it take?
items.why: The mark (four rounded bars and a dot) has two geometries. PR #58 moved the dot onto the centre of the bottom bar (`cy` 218.33 → 244.04) on the 2026-10-12 feedback, but only in the inline marks: the favicon, the restored hero stage and the share image still draw the old position. The wordmark is Geist in the site header and Newsreader on the share image, and in June Daniel liked a heavy knockout lockup (white mark and RICHVIEW in capitals on near-black), asking for more letter spacing.
items.proposed: One mark file, with the dot centred on the bottom bar (`cy=244.04` in its 268.58 × 269.73 box), drives the favicon, site header, hero, share images and social posts. On the site, share images, social posts and RichView's presentations it is the brand blue `#1A6DAC` on light surfaces and white on dark or blue ones; inside a report the wordmark takes its style's own shade of the brand blue (STY-01, STY-02). The wordmark is "RichView" in Geist 600 beside the mark. The knockout lockup — white mark and RICHVIEW in Geist 600 capitals, tracked wider, on a near-black block — is the heavy variant for dark surfaces and social images. Nothing else recolours, outlines or animates the mark except the landing story (STY-44).

items.title: Exactly five styles
items.question: Which styles exist: the five builtins only, or also the 20 studio variants and the showcase's own versions of three of them?
items.why: Three catalogues coexist. Core has five builtins under six names. The flagship showcase offers 23 treatments from a TypeScript-era stylesheet snapshot ("snapshot c617606"): Sleek, Scientific and Brutalist drawn differently from core (filled stat cards, callout side bars, mono stats at 2.5 rem, 62–66ch measures) plus 20 June studio variants, and no Sleek Light or Hand-drawn. Recomputed under today's neighbour rule, 16 of the 23 showcase palettes fail; only Sleek, v01, v02, v03, v07, v08 and v20 pass. Daniel's requests on extra styles changed twice: S27-594 (2026-10-05) asked for a dropdown of other themes, the 2026-10-12 feedback applied in PR #58 listed five themes with no dropdown, and S27-654 (2026-10-18) asked again for "Other styles".
items.proposed: RichView has exactly five styles: Sleek Dark, Sleek Light, Scientific, Brutalist and Hand-drawn. Every surface — CLI, MCP, playground, landing demo, docs and the flagship page — offers these five and renders them with the core styles. The 20 studio variants and the showcase's stylesheet snapshot (`assets/showcase/themes.css`, `themes.json`) are deleted; the design-system repository keeps them as history, and its `.rvstyle.yaml` export format is not adopted (TYP-93). The showcase-only chart keys leave with the snapshot: `dashes` and `symbols` (per-series line dashes and marker shapes) come from the decal rule (FEA-CH-57), and `measures` (a second colour set for non-company series) from the one palette. Whether a style pairs light and dark is STY-20's. A sixth style is added through a decision card in the review packet (DEL-06).

items.title: The palette rule
items.question: Are these the rules every categorical palette and ramp must pass, and do they cover every pair of the first four colours?
items.why: FEA-CH-62 checks every palette at render and leaves the values here. Code calls the rule "director decision D25" (and D26), defined nowhere else. It compares only neighbouring colours, yet any two series can meet in a chart. Recomputed on 2026-10-22, Scientific's first and third colours differ by ΔE×100 12.7 for normal vision and 2.6 under colour-vision simulation, and its second and fourth by 12.3; Brutalist (first and fourth, 6.6 simulated) and Hand-drawn (first and fourth 13.0, second and fourth 11.0) also fall below the floors. items.proposed: The palette rule, under that name: on the chart surface and the page, the first four colours of a categorical palette reach 3:1; every pair among the first four, and each neighbouring pair after them, differs by OKLab ΔE×100 of at least 15 for normal vision and 8 under protan, deutan and tritan simulation (Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes 2009, full severity); every colour lies inside sRGB. A ramp has three stops whose lightness moves steadily away from the surface, its high end at 3:1. A diverging ramp's two arms differ by the same 15 and 8 at their middle and high stops, or the style marks the sign another way (STY-56). Builtin palettes that fail are retuned, keeping their hue order. The labels "D25" and "D26" are retired.

items.title: A company colour derives a complete style
items.question: How can an author turn a company colour into a complete checked RichView style?
items.why: A brand style should be practical to make from a company guide without hand-tuning every token and chart colour. Existing style files allow individual colours and fonts, but the resulting palette can fail contrast or colour-vision checks. The shortcut extends STY-15 and STY-53 and the print counterpart follows STY-21.
items.proposed: A style file may name `company.color`, optional `company.secondary` and an optional builtin `company.base`. When the base is omitted, a builtin already named in the cascade remains; otherwise use Air. RichView derives subtly tinted surfaces, inks, accent, link and a six-slot series palette from the company colour and the chosen base. It does not change `tokens.brand`, the RichView wordmark colour (STY-01, STY-04). Achromatic inputs leave the base neutrals untinted. An accent or link that cannot meet its contrast floor moves toward a legible shade, and an info diagnostic names the input and result; the first series keeps the exact company colour when it reaches 3:1. A secondary colour that is insufficiently distinct is adjusted or omitted with an info diagnostic. An explicit token or palette in the file wins, and the normal checks measure the final cascade (STY-22, STY-25, STY-53, FEA-CH-62). A dark base derives its printed style over its light counterpart. The site Wasm exposes the same derivation to the live demo. `richview learn style` and a worked example teach the one-colour route.

items.title: A company name and logo travel with its style
items.question: How can a company style carry its logo safely into every report surface?
items.why: A reusable company style needs the company mark in reports, exports and shared links without opening the raw HTML or SVG boundary.
items.proposed: The `company` mapping may name `name`, `logo` and optional `logo-dark`. A logo is a report-relative still PNG, JPEG or WebP, identified from its bytes, at most 512 KiB and 1024 px on its longer side; APNG and animated WebP are refused. It uses the bounded report-folder resolver, including symlink containment. The company name supplies alt text; without a name the image is decorative and a warning asks for one. Show the logo before the report title and preserve it in exported HTML, PDFs and link-preview thumbnails. On a dark style use `logo-dark` when supplied, otherwise give the light logo its own light plate. Report frontmatter does not gain a logo field. Until logo rendering is implemented, these fields are experimental and say so. This extends STY-71 and preserves ARC-12 and ARC-13.
